name: Wraparound sunglasses

lead: Wraparound sunglasses use a strongly curved frame, often with a single curved lens or two lenses, so they follow the shape of the face. That gives coverage at the sides as well as the front, shielding the eye area from stray light.

For appearance, they are worn as a style statement: a sporty, futuristic or sleek frame, and one that hides the eye area and the skin around it from sun. The style has cycled in and out of fashion since the 1960s.

paras: People pick them for sport, driving in glare, skiing or everyday wear. Side coverage is the main feature; sport versions add impact-resistant lenses, straps and nose cushions. Lens UV rating matters more than lens darkness or price.

Dark lenses without UV protection let the pupil widen and can admit more UV than no lenses, according to the sunglasses article on Wikipedia. Side arms that are very deep can reduce peripheral vision.

chain: Curved frame covers sides of eyes
Blocks glare and sun around the eye area
Sleek, sporty look and a masked eye area
angle.text: They change how the upper face reads by covering the eyes and the surrounding skin, and they add a defined, sporty silhouette. People use them for both sun protection and style.

lead: Wraparound sunglasses are sunglasses with a strongly curved frame that wraps around the face, often with a single curved lens covering both eyes.[1] The shape provides coverage at the sides, which blocks stray light that would otherwise reach the eyes from the edges.[1][2]

People wear them for the sun protection around the eyes and for the look: a sporty, futuristic or streamlined frame that masks the eye area and adds a defined silhouette across the upper face. Wraparounds first appeared in the 1960s as aviator variants and were seen on Clint Eastwood in the Dirty Harry films and on Yoko Ono. A modern wrap style surged in the mid-1980s and became one of the favorite frames of the 1990s.[1]

The American Academy of Ophthalmology notes that wraparound styles give extra protection by blocking UV light that could enter from the sides, and that the label to look for is 100 percent UV protection or UV absorption up to 400 nm rather than lens darkness.[2] No studies found have measured how wraparound frames change perceived attractiveness; the research that exists concerns UV protection and eye health.[1][2]
infobox: Strongly curved frame, often one lens
Aviators, Wayfarers, glacier glasses, sport wraps

paras: A wraparound curves strongly to follow the face, sometimes with one continuous lens, and sits close enough to cover the temple side of the eye.[1] Sports variants add shatterproof, impact-resistant lenses, straps and nose cushions, and water versions may float or vent to prevent fogging.[1]

Related designs include glacier glasses, which use very dark round lenses with leather side blinders for mountaineering and snowfields.[1] The Academy of Ophthalmology adds that oversized lenses also give larger coverage, and that coloured or mirrored lenses mainly change style rather than UV protection.[2]

The sunglasses article places the first wraparounds in the 1960s as variants of the aviator, worn by figures such as Clint Eastwood in the Dirty Harry films and Yoko Ono.[1] A modern version, derived from the Wayfarer but with a more futuristic look, became popular in the mid-1980s and a favorite frame of the 1990s after a reaction against 1980s fashion.[1]

The sport-eyewear branch has its own lineage. Oakley, founded by Jim Jannard in 1975 in his garage, moved from motorcycle grips into goggles and in 1984 introduced Factory Pilot Eyeshades, sport sunglasses that resembled goggles; it later grew into a company bought by Luxottica in 2007 for 2.1 billion dollars.[3] Sunglasses in general have a longer background, from Inuit snow goggles to the 1929 celluloid frames sold by Sam Foster and the 1936 polarizing filter developed by Edwin Land.[1]

Wraparounds give side coverage, which offers protection from stray light, and larger frames cover more skin around the eyes.[1][2] Style writers and wearers treat them as a sporty counterpart to aviators and Wayfarers.[1]

In looksmaxxing terms, the frame is a way to shape how the upper third of the face reads: it conceals the eye area, adds a continuous horizontal line and can be matched to face shape. Users who care about the skin around the eyes also value the side coverage for the same reason the eye-health bodies cite it, reduced sun reaching the periorbital area.[2]

Experts quoted in the sunglasses article recommend lenses that block at least 99% of UVA and UVB up to 400 nm (UV400); price and lens colour do not reliably indicate protection. Dark lenses lacking UV filtering can be more harmful than none because the pupil dilates.[1] The AAO likewise says darker lenses do not necessarily offer more protection and that polarization alone does not block UV.[2]

Standards include the international ISO 12312, the EU EN 1836:2005 and the US ANSI Z80.3.[1] Deep side arms can block peripheral vision, and UK guidance advises against them for driving; category 4 lenses are labeled not suitable for driving.[1] Sunglasses do not protect against looking directly at the sun, including during an eclipse.[1]
No studies found. A related trial of amber blue-light-blocking lenses worn in lightweight wraparound frames before bed examined sleep in people with insomnia, not appearance.[4]
